stories.summary: The co-pilot of flydubai flight ⁠FZ1073 attempted to carry out a "terrorist" attack during the flight, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said, according ⁠to the state news agency WAM. The co-pilot attacked the pilot inside the cockpit ‌with an axe and attempted to ⁠take control ‌of the aircraft, the prosecutor general said. Investigations ⁠are ‌ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the ⁠motives and any related ⁠connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, he added. The co-pilot had previously been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views, multiple media outlets reported. Scrutiny into the alleged assailant - who was identified in the reports as Omani national Hamam al-Hammami - and his motives has intensified after Wednesday's incident aboard a Dubai-Tel Aviv route that officials say narrowly avoided catastrophe. stories.title: Gardaí treating death of woman in balcony fall as assault
stories.summary: The woman who died in hospital on Wednesday following a fall from a balcony in north Dublin has been named as Kathleen Carey. The incident, which gardaí are treating as a serious assault, took place near Main Street in Belmayne, Dublin 13 on Monday afternoon. Ms Carey was brought to Beaumont Hospital for treatment and died from her injuries on Wednesday. A post-mortem examination has been carried out, the results of which will determine the course of the investigation. A man aged in his 20s was arrested on Tuesday in connection with the incident. He was released without charge yesterday and a file has been sent to the Director of Public Prosecutions.

stories.title: PBP proposes tax on millionaires, corporation tax hike
stories.summary: People Before Profit is proposing a new tax on multi-millionaires as well as increasing the corporation tax to 20% as part of its alternative budget package. The document - entitled A Radical Budget for an Affordable Ireland - also proposes a €500 electricity credit for every household funded by a levy on data centres. TD Richard Boyd Barrett said taxing wealth and multinational businesses would raise an additional €45bn to go towards tackling the cost-of-living and housing crises. "The idea of taxing wealth and big business in order to address the cost of living and housing misery is an idea whose time has come. "If we make the multimillionaires and the big corporations and the energy companies and the data centers pay some additional taxes, we can protect people from the housing misery, from the cost-of-living misery," Mr Boyd Barrett said. His party colleague, TD Paul Murphy said the Irish people should not accept being "held hostage to the demands of US corporations that are using Ireland as a conduit to a corporate tax haven".

stories.title: Irish Mist sale sees brand return to Irish ownership
stories.summary: Co Offaly-based drinks brand Irish Mist has been sold by US company Heaven Hill Brands to Dublin-based drinks business, the Old Canal Quay Spirits company. The Old Canal Quay Spirits company is owned and led by international spirits industry specialist and entrepreneur David Phelan and fellow Irish drinks industry figures. He is one of the two men behind the sale of the Boru Vodka/Castle Brands which he co-founded with Pat Rigney, from The Shed Distillery, in 1998. David Phelan will lead the Irish Mist's growth and development as CEO of the Old Canal Quay Spirits company. He is backed by investors including Pat Rigney, and Tom Cleary, who owns The Temple Bar in Dublin, along with US-based premium wine and spirits company Blue Ridge Spirits and Wine marketing. Both Phelan and Rigney have a strong connection to the famous Irish whiskey liqueur, having worked together developing and growing the brand after it was sold to C&C in the 1980s. The US is the biggest market for Irish Mist, which was founded in the 1940s.

stories.title: Israeli officials to question flydubai attack co-pilot
stories.summary: Israeli officials are expected to question the co-pilot who allegedly attempted to crash a commercial passenger flight from Dubai bound for Tel Aviv, according to a source briefed on the investigation. Disaster was averted on flydubai flight FZ1073 on Wednesday after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had stabbed the captain in what Israeli officials have said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying 174 passengers and crew. A reserve flydubai pilot crew travelling on the flight landed the plane at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi Arabian authorities. The co-pilot was transferred yesterday to the UAE, where the source said Israeli officials were expected to question him. The source declined to say which Israeli agency or authority would take part in the questioning. Asked whether Israeli officials would question the co-pilot, an Israeli government official told Reuters that Israeli investigators would take part in the UAE-led investigation alongside Emirati authorities, seeking to determine what happened and examine the suspect's motives and background.

stories.title: GPA seeks extra €700 a year per inter-county player
stories.summary: The Gaelic Players' Association (GPA) has asked Government for an extra €700 per player a year in support to help with what their CEO Tom Parsons described as "cost of living pressures". Inter-county players and representatives from the GPA met with Minister for Sport Patrick O'Donovan on Wednesday to seek the increase as part of the association's pre-budget engagement with Government. In total the GPA is seeking an additional €2.8m investment, which would bring support up from €1,800 to €2,500 per player. "Government funding is an important recognition of the extraordinary commitment made by inter-county players to our national games," said Parsons. "The findings presented to the Minister today give a clear picture of the reality behind that commitment. "At a time when the cost of living pressures are bearing down on players, Government has an opportunity to deliver something immediate and tangible for the current generation. We are asking for an additional €700 a year per player, bringing the support to €2,500.

stories.title: When the Girls in Green first went to Kazakhstan
stories.summary: Seventeen years ago, the Republic of Ireland women's team ventured into the unknown for a World Cup double-header against Russia and Kazakhstan. The Girls in Green had previously been to Russia in 2005, when they lost 5-1 (Michele O'Brien got the consolation goal). But they'd never played a senior international in Kazakhstan. Noel King's team beat the Kazakhs 2-1 in Turner's Cross thanks to a late goal from young Raheny United striker Stephanie Roche, so they travelled with some confidence in their quest to reach the 2011 World Cup in Germany. It was October 2009. I Gotta Feeling by the Black Eyed Peas was No 1 in the Irish charts, Brian Cowen was Taoiseach, and the country was mourning the death of Boyzone's Stephen Gately. The Ireland squad included Katie Taylor; a tough-tackling 23-year-old midfielder with a burning ambition to build a boxing career. Taylor had been in the senior setup since 2006 having come through the underage ranks. Football was a release from the isolated intensity of boxing training, and she was talented enough to keep her place despite often missing training sessions due to commitments in the ring.

stories.title: Cullen backs Henshaw as back-row cover in Durban
stories.summary: Leinster head coach Leo Cullen has backed Ireland international centre Robbie Henshaw to do a job in the back-row, if he is called upon on Saturday. The defending URC champions are in Durban to take on the Sharks, but injuries in camp have forced them to go bold on the bench. With Scott Penny and Max Deegan having flown home to Dublin due to injury, Cullen has taken a punt on 33-year-old Henshaw to be the hybrid forward if needed, despite starting at inside centre. Speaking to the media on Thursday, Cullen outlined the thought process behind the move. "We've seen Robbie do that role for us last season without really any prep. This week we've actually managed to get a bit of prep into him," he explained. "He'll be able to cover that if needs be. Brian Deeney can cover the (number) six role as well, a few different options there, which we've played around with this week.

stories.title: MusicTown celebrates Phil Lynott's life and legacy, 40 years on
stories.summary: Phil Lynott, the much loved Dubliner, musician, lead singer of Thin Lizzy and cultural icon, died forty years ago in 1986. To mark 40 years since his passing, MusicTown at the National Concert Hall in Dublin, supported by Dublin City Council, is presenting a programme of events celebrating and reflecting on his life and times under the title Philo-sophy Talks. The events include talks on his early recordings tonight (Friday October 2nd), a concert in his old school in Crumlin tomorrow (Saturday October 3rd), and an exhibition entitled 'Lost Love Of Romeo' at Studio 10 on Wicklow Street across the weekend. For his old friend and collaborator, the artist Jim Fitzpatrick, this week's events have been an enjoyable trip down memory lane. Celebrated for his unique visual style, Fitzpatrick designed iconic album covers for several Thin Lizzy albums, which are on display. He said that he could "only imagine standing here with Philip Lynott looking at this exhibition. He would be in his element." He went on to say that "Philip was one of those wonderful friends... we were more than just friends, we were collaborators."

stories.summary: This Morning presenter Alison Hammond disappeared from the programme in the middle of the show on Friday as she felt "a little unwell". Hammond has since provided an update on social media saying that she had her heart "checked out" after experiencing a "palpitation" but assured fans she is "fine". "Hello, my lovelies. I know you’re all worried about me," she said.

stories.title: Major public safety operation continues in Portadown
stories.summary: A major public safety operation will continue in Portadown over the weekend, the PSNI has said, as the stand-off between the Orange Order and Garvaghy Road residents over a contentious parade continues. The Portadown District of the unionist Orange Order wants to complete its traditional route for the first time in almost 30 years after the Parades Commission ruled they should be allowed along the Garvaghy Road, but the coalition of residents in the largely nationalist area is opposed to the march going ahead. Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said that police "will do everything we can to maintain order and ensure the safety of everyone in that area". It comes as Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Byrant called for calm and said his door remains open for talks. "Everyone across Northern Ireland wants a peaceful resolution to the situation in Portadown," he wrote on X. "I’m continuing to work to find a mutually acceptable agreement and I’m grateful to everyone who has offered help and has taken part in the discussions so far.

stories.title: Man on bail who stabbed friend jailed for 6 further years
stories.summary: A man described as a 'Jekyll and Hyde' has received a six-year jail sentence for stabbing a former friend seven times while he was on bail for a vicious attack on his ex-partner. Athlone father-of-two Mark Conway's latest sentence, handed down this morning, is to run consecutively to a five-year, three-month sentence imposed in January. The 40-year-old sliced his victim's liver, resulting in emergency surgery, and his gallbladder had to be removed, Mullingar Circuit Criminal Court heard. Later, he and his terrified family had to endure local taunts that Conway was like the fictional horror film character Freddy Krueger and that he "was coming for you". Conway pleaded guilty to causing serious harm, and other charges connected to the vicious knife attack on 1 March 2025. Gardaí arrived to find blood trails from the stab victim leading to each man's home, in Marine View, Athlone, Co Westmeath.

stories.title: SDLP selects new candidate for Justin McNulty seat
stories.summary: Councillor Peter Byrne will contest Newry and Armagh for the SDLP in next year's Assembly convention, replacing Justin McNulty. Mr Byrne, a councillor for 10 years, was chosen in a selection convention of party members. He runs a business in Crossmaglen, where he lives with his husband. Following his selection, he said he wants to be "a relentless champion for Newry and Armagh". In an apparent reference to the Drumcree dispute, he added: "If the past week teaches us anything, it is that we need to move forward and do politics differently. "For the SDLP, that means making things work today whilst planning for a new Ireland in the future, and I am looking forward to taking this message to the people of Newry and Armagh in the weeks and months ahead."

stories.title: Euro zone inflation surges, keeping pressure on ECB
stories.summary: Euro zone inflation surged more than expected in September and is likely to increase further in the coming months on soaring energy costs, keeping pressure on the European Central Bank to raise interest rates and governments to help struggling consumers. Inflation in the 21 nations sharing the euro currency jumped to 3.8% in September from 3.2% a month earlier, exceeding expectations for 3.6% in a Reuters poll, driven primarily by fuel, natural gas, and to a lesser extent, food costs. A closely watched 'core' figure, which excludes volatile food and fuel prices and signals underlying trends, accelerated to 2.5% from 2.4%, on a pick-up in services prices, data from Eurostat, the EU's statistics agency, showed today. Rising fuel costs are putting pressure on European governments to support households and businesses, and in some countries such as France have already triggered street protests, potentially stretching already precarious public finances. While subsidies have been minor so far, totalling around 0.1% of the bloc's GDP, they are less targeted and temporary than hoped, suggesting more lasting budget pain. For the ECB, the figures are likely to be seen as a mixed bag.

stories.title: Hundreds of French high schools shut amid protests
stories.summary: French high school students have lit fires outside schools and faced off with police as a protest movement that has forced the closure of some 400 establishments showed no sign of abating. The movement, which began last week in the Paris region and rapidly spread nationwide, has seen teenage pupils at lycees in their final years of schooling block access to buildings and clash with police. The students say their school hours are excessively long, conditions inadequate including overheated classrooms, and that there are too many staff absences. The government says the grievances are legitimate but has condemned what it has described as "urban violence". Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing tear gas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris today, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools - Leonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the southeast - with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes, an AFP photographer said.

stories.title: Bohemians keep title bid on track with win at Oriel Park
stories.summary: Bohemians put themselves firmly in contention for their first league title since 2009 as they moved joint-top of the SSE Airtricity Men's Premier Division table by holding out for a huge three points against Dundalk at Oriel Park. A first half penalty from Colm Whelan and a 68th minute strike from Ross Tierney looked to have Alan Reynolds men cruising to victory, but a Daryl Horgan penalty two minutes from the end followed by the dismissal of Cian Byrne for a last man challenge a minute later set up a nervous finish, in which the home side hit the crossbar. In the end the Gypsies held out for a huge win that sees them go second in the table, ahead of Shamrock Rovers but just behind St Patrick’s Athletic on goal difference. The destiny of the title is now very much in the Phibsborough outfit’s hands as they face both of their Dublin rivals in their four remaining league matches. Before that, they have a chance of making the FAI Cup final, with a semi-final at home to Waterford FC to come next Friday. Bohs released a statement after the match stating that they would not be engaging in any media requests for the remainder of the season in protest at the league’s decision to bring forward Shamrock Rovers’ tie with Drogheda United next Thursday by 24 hours. With the Gypsies in cup semi-final action on Friday, 9 October, it means Rovers have an extra day’s rest before their league showdown on Monday, 12 October.

stories.title: Emerging star McAllister looking to finish 2026 on a high
stories.summary: It has been some time since any Ulster player has had such an immediate impact on the inter-county camogie scene as Éobha McAllister. The Dunloy teenager scored on her debut as a second half substitute in the opening Division 1A game against Tipperary and contributed handsomely in every other game of Antrim's season that delivered a first win over Cork in 70 years, a third successive Ulster title and an All-Ireland intermediate crown in August. Just 11 days after the Croke Park showdown with Laois when she scored five points, Antrim’s new kid on the block registered a last quarter hat-trick as well as six earlier points to take Dunloy from two points down at the break against visitors Ballycastle to a comfortable win in the opening round of the Antrim senior championship. After the round robin group stages of the club title-race, McAllister is well ahead of the chasing pack in the race to become the championship’s top-scorer. This is semi-finals weekend and Dunloy will again face Ballycastle while Loughgiel, chasing a 13th successive crown, take on Cushendall. Everyone is talking about the youngster who this week, was named as one of three nominees for the PwC Camogie All-Ireland intermediate Player of the Year award. Her inclusion in the Soaring Stars team was a given.

stories.title: Munster Rugby chief executive Flanagan to depart
stories.summary: Munster Rugby chief executive Ian Flanagan has confirmed he will resign from his position at the end of the month. Flanagan's position has been under scrutiny in recent months after a number of controversies in the organisation, leading to calls for "change" at the top of Munster Rugby from a number of former players. "Munster Rugby and the IRFU today confirm that Ian Flanagan has informed the Board of Munster Rugby of his decision to step down from his position as CEO at the end of October," a statement from the province said. "An Interim CEO will be announced in the coming weeks and a recruitment process for a permanent successor will be undertaken in due course." Flanagan's resignation arrives just over four months since Munster commissioned an independent review into the governance of their organisation after a damaging period for the province off the pitch, the findings of which have yet to be made public. In March, the province confirmed they would be seeking a number of voluntary redundancies, before further controversy followed in April, with the decision to appoint Roger Randle as attack coach.

stories.title: On love, loss and belonging in nature - Eoin Warner's new memoir
stories.summary:
In January 1979, when Eoin Warner was two years old, an oil tanker exploded in Bantry Bay. Among the fifty lives lost was Eoin's father. This devastating event cast a long shadow, shaping a childhood in which grief was a quiet presence at the table and in the empty front seat of the car. During this time, Eoin discovered how the natural world reflects so much of our human story, and it became his refuge. This memoir is not a straight line through loss; it's a series of vivid encounters with
the natural world, brimming with enchantment and wonder. In May 2010, a vixen appeared in Booterstown. What was fascinating about this visitor was that she would wander around in the revealing light of day, no doubt driven by a hungry litter of cubs. She would slip along the edge of the path in front of the houses and walk, Houdini-like, through the railings of our gate to visit our garden. We used to watch from the window, enthralled by this wild visitor as she sniffed the empty dog bowl and the hens, who were safe in their run. On one surreal occasion, the vixen even flirted with Mac. Although she was smaller than him, he was delighted by the female attention. They played for ages, running rings around each other on the small lawn. Mac had a bit of a roving eye. A relaxed human leg or a vixen were all fair game in his mind. Adaptation to environmental change is a natural part of evolution, a process that unfolds over generations in which the strongest survive. Unfortunately, in this epoch of human-induced environmental change, the pace is so rapid that many species cannot adapt quickly enough to survive. Some species, however, are adjusting and leveraging the skills they already possess to adapt to this rapidly changing landscape. The red fox (Vulpes vulpes) is one. Their natural range spans extreme climates across the whole northern hemisphere, where they have made almost every habitat their home. Historically, the shy fox has preferred to avoid human contact and has made its home in rural settings. However, as we encroach on the foxes' habitat with our growing towns and cities, making their habitat ours, they adapt, moving into our urban areas. Take a night-time drive at any time of year through the lamp-lit streets of Dublin and you are almost guaranteed to see a fox moving in the shadows. On a warm June evening, the front door was open and the vixen walked into the house, meeting me in the living room. We both stopped dead in our tracks, six feet apart, and stared at each other. I was startled, as I’m sure she was, but if so, she certainly did not show it. She stared at me with emotionless amber eyes, her gaze examining me. Her sharply cocked ears were faced squarely in my direction and didn’t move. She looked incongruous among the brightly coloured blue and yellow toys. Once she grew bored of our staring contest, she turned and left without even a courtesy glance back. It was the strangest feeling, as if this were an affront. The fox has taught me to honour these shared spaces, so that I now acknowledge I am entering another's space – the more-than-human world. Now, whenever I enter a woodland, a bog or the sea, I pause and remind myself that I am the visitor.

stories.title: Freddie Mercury's notebook sells for €322,000 at auction
stories.summary: A notebook containing the late Freddie Mercury's song lyrics has sold for £277,000 (€321,000) at auction. The handwritten lyrics by the Queen frontman were the highest-selling lot on day one of Propstore’s Music Live Auction. The lyrics were from the recording sessions for Mercury’s debut solo album, Mr. Bad Guy, which was released in 1985. They formed part of The Reinhold Mack Collection, an archive of handwritten lyrics, recording memorabilia and personal gifts documenting the producer’s close friendship and creative partnership with Mercury. Noel Gallagher’s autographed Takamine FP460SC acoustic guitar, which he owned and played during Oasis’s 1996 MTV Unplugged performance, set a world record for the highest price achieved at auction for an Oasis acoustic guitar, selling for £226,800 (€263,000). stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (October 2-4)
stories.summary: From Halloween headpieces to Baroque A Cappella, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. BuzzFest - Phibsboro's Community, Sustainability & Biodiversity Festival - returns for its 10th year on Saturday, 3 October. The festival will run from 12.30pm to 4pm in the Scouts Hall (located behind the library) with an amazing selection of stalls, stands, talks, workshops, repair cafe, music, food and craic. This includes a Halloween headpiece workshop inspired by collage art and fuelled by love for scavenging. All materials provided. The workshop will last 40 minutes and is aimed at those 6+. Tickets €2 on Eventbrite. Eatyard brings a slice of Bavaria to Drumcondra this October, with a series of beers*, pretzels, music, bands, fun & games running from Sept 24th - Oct 24th at The Bernard Shaw. Expect a whole host of German games to dig your teeth into, including Stein-Holding competitions, Hasselhoff karaoke, Lederhösen Limbo, the spicy currywurst challenge, live music & much more. Tickets €16.97 on Eventbrite. The event is for those 20+. Dublin Mountains Festival (Féile na Sléibhte) runs from 1-10 October, celebrating nature through community-driven events. On Friday, 2 October, a walk and talk with tree planting at Barnaslingan Wood will take place, led by the Coillte team overseeing the Dublin Mountains Makeover project. Reserve a spot on Eventbrite. Mother x Absolut present Daytime Dance Party: The Doll Edition On Saturday, 3 October, The George will play host to a very special edition of the Daytime Dance Party series. Trans, intersex and non-binary people will be celebrated with a jam-packed lineup including Glamo, Shrem, Mars Montana, Ruth Kavanagh, Shaqira Knightly, Toni & Tony, Dr Count Evil, Anziety, and Queeen Marie. Tickets are €5.58, with ticket revenue going to the Transgender Equality Network Ireland.

stories.title: Govt breaking its promise on spending increases
stories.summary: Last year, Minister for Finance Simon Harris and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers promised the days of continuous spending overruns were at an end. Their message was that the party was over for departments and ministers who had overseen enormous surges in spending over recent years. Minister Harris said expenditure allocations were being increased and "departments now need to live within those budgets". Minister Chambers said that continuous spending overruns, by departments that could not operate within their means, had to come to an end. The two ministers published a Medium Term Fiscal and Structural Plan, which set out expenditure ceilings for each year. In 2026, spending was supposed to be limited to an increase of 7%. That was an enormous rise, bigger than any expenditure increase in any other EU country.
stories.rssSummary: Ireland was supposed to limit spending increases to 7% in 2026, but the Government is failing to meet its own already enormous target and using windfall taxes to cover the overrun.

stories.title: TUI members to strike over pay deal delay
stories.summary: Members of the Teachers' Union of Ireland (TUI) have voted overwhelmingly in favour of industrial action, up to and including strike action, over delays in agreeing a new public sector pay deal. The TUI represents over 23,000 members in post-primary, further and higher education. They will begin industrial action in the form of a work-to-rule from Monday 12 October. They will also join other public sector workers for an all-out strike on Wednesday 14 October and Wednesday 21 October. "We urge the Government to engage meaningfully with union representatives to negotiate a fair pay agreement for public servants," said TUI General Secretary Michael Gillespie. "Should they fail to do so, our campaign of industrial action, emphatically endorsed by membership, will continue," Mr Gillespie said.

stories.title: SF alternative budget targets living costs, second homes
stories.summary: Sinn Féin is proposing a permanent ten cent reduction in petrol and diesel as well as extending excise cuts for another six months as part of its €13.4 billion alternative budget package. The 40-page document, entitled 'Putting workers and families first', proposes the Government not proceed with planned carbon tax increases, remove all excise on home heating oil and reduce green diesel by 17 cent for a minimum of six months. The proposed measures to help reduce fuel costs for households run to €1.5 billion with the expense of cutting 10c off petrol and diesel at the pumps for the next year running to €404 million. As per last year, Sinn Féin is proposing an emergency cost of living package. This would include an "Everyday Essential Card" - a preloaded card with €500 for one million households most in need to spend on groceries - and the extension of the back-to-school clothing and footwear allowance to every child in the country. The party would also provide €400 in energy credits for householders. Sinn Féin would also abolish student fees, halt public transport fare increases and introduce a new tier of child benefit to target those most at risk of poverty.

stories.title: Ryanair cancelled over 1,000 flights due to ATC issues
stories.summary: Ryanair has partly blamed the recent "collapse" in Britain's air traffic control system for cancelling more than 1,000 flights in September. The airline said the cancellations were due to two air traffic control (ATC) issues in the UK within a fortnight of each other last month, as well as ATC strikes in Belgium and disruption across Europe due to volcanic ash clouds from Mount Etna eruptions. The boss of Britain's National Air Traffic Services (Nats), Martin Rolfe, has come under pressure to step down after a spate of air traffic issues caused thousands of flights to be cancelled across the industry last month, impacting hundreds of thousands of passengers. The most recent was caused by a "connectivity issue" at its Prestwick centre in Scotland, which was unrelated to an ATC software fault on September 8, which caused widespread flight chaos. Ryanair has been among those calling for Mr Rolfe to resign and Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander has called a meeting with Nats chairman Warren East, the former chief executive of Rolls-Royce, in the coming weeks to discuss the problems. Ryanair's latest traffic figures showed it operated over 111,700 flights last month and carried 20.1 million passengers, up 4% year on year.

stories.title: Russian attacks 'tearing Kyiv apart' - city Mayor
stories.summary: Russian attacks on key infrastructure are "tearing Kyiv apart", according to the city's mayor, as strikes on a bridge linking the capital's east and west brought traffic to a standstill. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has accused Russian President Vladimir Putin of ripping up the rulebook of armed conflict by sanctioning massive attacks on civilian areas, an accusation the Kremlin has rejected. The war, which began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, has largely focused on ground fighting in the east, with Kyiv largely spared from the devastation near the frontline. However, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko has said that the city should now be on a war footing. "The capital is in a very dramatic situation," he posted on Telegram. "It's no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we lived in peacetime.

stories.title: Frawley marks Connacht debut with match-winning try
stories.summary: Debutant Ciarán Frawley's 77th-minute try helped Connacht open their account in the new United Rugby Championship with a 22-19 victory at Benetton. After the Irish outfit lost at home to Stormers last weekend, Stuart Lancaster’s side were heading for another defeat with Benetton able to open up a narrow two-point lead thanks to Bautista Bernasconi’s score early in the second half. However, Frawley followed up a fine first try for the club with a slick finish after an excellent team move to spark jubilant scenes in Italy after a last-gasp win. Only five minutes were on the clock in Treviso when Cian Prendergast put Connacht ahead, but it sparked a frantic opening 40. Benetton immediately replied through Bernasconi before Sean O’Brien restored the visitors lead, but Leonardo Marin’s try and a successful conversion by Jacob Umaga put the hosts on front with 35 played. Frawley had other ideas with a 37th-minute score backed up with two points by Sam Gilbert and while Bernasconi’s try after 51 minutes ensured Benetton held the lead for long periods of the second half, a brilliant move finished with three minutes left earned Lancaster’s men a bonus-point triumph.
